content.text: The Chrome extension isn't connected. Let me check the Owletto extension path (per `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`) and simultaneously check whether prod is actually serving Slack/Telegram traffic — the fastest ground truth is the prod DB.

input.command: sed -n '1,80p' docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md

result.output:
# Browser-driven verification (authenticated)

For any UI verification that needs a signed-in session (past the auth wall), use the `agent-browser` CLI with a session cookie minted from the DB. The user's regular Chrome doesn't expose a remote-debug port, so `--auto-connect` will land on the wrong tab — mint a cookie instead.

## Scope

The forged session cookie authenticates the **web admin REST mounted at `/`** (`/api/auth/*`, `/api/<orgSlug>/...`, the SPA — anything `lobu apply` and the web app talk to). It does **NOT** authenticate the **public Agent API at `/lobu`** (`/lobu/api/v1/agents/*`, `/lobu/api/v1/agents/<id>/sessions`) — that path expects a JWT bearer from the OAuth device flow (`lobu login`) or a PAT. If `/lobu/api/v1/agents` returns `401` despite a valid cookie, switch to `lobu chat` / `lobu token`.

## Pick a target

Local dev backend (with prod DB attached over Tailscale): `https://<your-tailscale-host>.ts.net:8443`. Prod: `https://app.lobu.ai`.

## Grab the secret + session token

```bash
# Local dev backend uses .env's BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
SECRET=$(grep '^BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

# Prod uses the secret on the K8s pod
SECRET=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod \
  $(kubectl get pod -n summaries-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu-app -o name | head -1 | sed 's|pod/||') \
  -- printenv BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)

# Session token from the DB (prod DB serves both targets)
DB="$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
TOKEN=$(psql "$DB" -tAc "SELECT token FROM session WHERE \"userId\" = '<user_id>' AND \"expiresAt\" > NOW() ORDER BY \"updatedAt\" DESC LIMIT 1")
```

## Sign the cookie

better-auth uses HMAC-SHA256, base64, then URL-encode — base64**url** does *not* validate.

```bash
SIGNED=$(SECRET="$SECRET" TOKEN="$TOKEN" node -e '
  const {createHmac}=require("node:crypto");
  const sig=createHmac("sha256",process.env.SECRET).update(process.env.TOKEN).digest("base64");
  console.log(encodeURIComponent(`${process.env.TOKEN}.${sig}`));
')
```

Cookie name is `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` whenever the baseURL is `https://` (prod and Tailscale dev qualify; only plain-http localhost uses the unprefixed `better-auth.session_token`).

## Drive the browser

```bash
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify eval "document.cookie='__Secure-better-auth.session_token=$SIGNED; path=/; secure; samesite=lax'"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/<path>"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify wait --text "<expected text>" --timeout 25000
agent-browser --session lobu-verify snapshot -i      # find @refs
agent-browser --session lobu-verify click @e13        # interact
agent-browser --session lobu-verify screenshot --full /tmp/out.png
agent-browser --session lobu-verify close
```

## Driving the paired Owletto extension (connector debugging)

The cookie-forging above and `claude-in-chrome` both drive a *separate* browser that lacks the user's real logged-in sessions — Revolut, for instance, redirects them to `sso.revolut.com/signin`. To run JS or browser actions in the **paired Owletto extension** (the Chrome that holds the user's live sessions, which is what extension-scrape connectors like Revolut/LinkedIn use), go through the connector-operations bridge instead. No deploy required.

`lobu connector run` is the wrong tool here — it only does local Playwright/CDP against a `browser_session` auth profile, so it errors `Missing --auth-profile` for device-worker connectors (Revolut has no auth profile).

For one-off actions, the `lobu call` CLI is the quickest path (usually org `buremba`; connection id from `lobu call manage_connections --org buremba --arg action=list --raw`):

```bash
lobu call manage_operations --org buremba --arg action=execute \
  --arg connection_id=<chrome-connection-id> --arg operation_key=navigate \
  --arg input:='{"url":"https://app.slack.com/...","wait_for_load":true,"open_in_new_tab":true}' --raw
```

For multi-step scripts, use the SDK `operations` namespace via `lobu memory exec` / `run_sdk`:

```js
// chrome connection id: client.connections.list() → connector_key 'chrome'
const ops = await client.operations.listAvailable({ connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID });
// navigate opens a fresh background tab in the paired Chrome and returns tab_id
const nav = await client.operations.execute({
  connection_id: CHROME_CONN_ID, operation_key: 'navigate',
  input: { url: 'https://app.revolut.com/transactions', open_in_new_tab: true, wait_for_load: true },
});
// evaluate runs arbitrary JS on that tab and returns the JSON-serialised result

I also validated your token before using it (`getMe` returned the bot cleanly), and there was no pre-existing webhook to clobber.

**One real bug found along the way, and it's worth your attention.** My first attempt used `client.connections.connect()`. It returned `status: "active"`, `facets.chat: true`, and **no error message** — but the connection was completely inert: no webhook registered, no `secretToken`, no `chatMetadata`. It only surfaced when binding the agent failed with *"this connection has no chat runtime"* — while the same row simultaneously reported `facets.chat: true`. That's a contradiction the API should not be able to produce.

The cause is that only `connections.create()` routes through `manage_connections` → `handleCreate`, which detects `x-lobu-chat-platform` and calls `upsertByoChatConnection()` (`chat-connection-service.ts:235`) — the function that validates the token, generates the webhook secret, and registers with Telegram. `connections.connect()` just writes a DB row and reports success. So **an `active` chat connection is not evidence of a running runtime**, and anyone (or any agent) using `connect()` for a chat connector gets a silently dead bot. I deleted the inert row (458) and recreated via `create()`.

The last hop needs you — I have no Telegram account, so I can't send a message as a user. **DM `@burembalobubot` and tell me what comes back.** Expect one of two outcomes: a real answer from `personal-agent`, or the same `z.ai 429 Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted` error blocking Slack until 07-31. I used your browser and sent the messages. **Telegram is broken — and it's a different bug than the Slack one.**

I drove your real Chrome via the Owletto bridge to `web.telegram.org`, opened `@burembalobubot`, clicked START (sending `/start` at 04:19), then sent "hello, which agent are you?". **Neither got any reply**, 10+ minutes on.

The important part is where it breaks. I ruled out the obvious suspects:

- **Telegram delivered successfully.** `getWebhookInfo` shows `pending_update_count: 0` and, critically, **no `last_error_message` / `last_error_date`**. Telegram only omits those fields when your endpoint returns 2xx. So Lobu received both updates and ACKed them.
- **The route is live and correctly secured.** An unauthenticated POST to the webhook returns **401, not 404** — the connection resolves and the secret-token check works.
- **It is NOT the Z_AI 429.** I tested the bound agent directly: `conversations.send({agent_id: "personal-agent", text: "reply with the single word: pong"})` returned `status: "complete", reply: "pong"` in 3.4 seconds with no quota error. The `buremba` org's inference is fine; the 429 blocking Slack is a separate, unrelated problem in `lobu-crm`.

So: Telegram delivers → Lobu accepts and returns 2xx → nothing happens. The message is swallowed after ingestion.

The worst part is that it's **completely silent**. Connection 459 still reports `status: active`, `error_message: null`, `unhealthy_alerted_at: null`, and zero `channel_messages` rows for `platform='telegram'` — the inbound was never even recorded. Contrast with Slack, which surfaced its provider failure as a visible in-channel message with a CTA. A Telegram user gets no reply and no error, and you get no health signal.

Combined with the `connect()` bug from earlier, there are now two independent silent-failure modes on this path: a chat connection can look `active` while having no runtime, and a delivered message can vanish with no trace.

What I could not isolate from outside: whether the chat runtime instance for stable ID `85045b7a87884eea` actually started on the prod pod, or whether the update is parsed and then dropped. That needs prod gateway logs — `kubectl` has no cluster access from this machine, so I can't get them myself.

content.text:
Short answer: **we fixed a different drop than the one that's biting.**

I checked instead of guessing. #2257 ("reply with an unlinked notice on non-Slack platforms **instead of dropping**", fixes #2230) is real, it's about exactly this symptom, and it **is deployed** — prod is on revision `049ee2ab`, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor 5bc459084 049ee2ab` confirms the fix is in. Prod even rebuilt at 04:16, three minutes before my first test. So the fix is live and the message still vanished.

The reason it doesn't help: #2257 only covers the **"no agent resolved"** dead end. My connection *has* `agent_id: personal-agent`, so `resolveAgentId()` returns non-null (`platform-helpers.ts:206` — it returns `{source:"connection"}` whenever `agentId` is set) and execution never reaches the unlinked-notice site that #2257 patched. We fixed the unrouted path; this is the **routed** path failing.

I walked every drop site I could reach statically, and ruled each one out:

- The `!isPreview` guard at `message-handler-bridge.ts:789` — my connection's settings are `{allowGroups: true}`, no `previewMode`, so it's false.
- The "Behavior subscription but none matched" drop at :757 — needs a subscription, which a fresh DM has no reason to have.
- The fallback-link materialization at :855 — explicitly non-fatal and group-only; this is a DM.
- Stale/missing in-memory instance — `handleWebhook` (`chat-instance-manager.ts:1379`) re-hydrates per request and returns **404** when there's no instance. Telegram reports no error, so we returned 2xx: the instance existed and the adapter accepted the payload.

Three messages now (`/start` 04:19, "hello, which agent are you?", "retest 0330 after rebuild"), all delivered with `pending_update_count: 0` and **no `last_error_message`** — Telegram only omits that on a 2xx. And the agent itself is healthy: `conversations.send({agent_id:"personal-agent"})` returns "pong" in 3.4s.

So it's accepted, ACKed, and dropped after routing succeeds — a drop site I can't see from the source alone.

What I'd need to close it: **prod gateway logs for stable ID `85045b7a87884eea`**. The handler logs `"Routing to connection's owning agent"` on success — if that line is present, the break is downstream in dispatch; if it's absent, the message never reached the bridge and the break is in the adapter/webhook layer. That single grep splits the remaining space in half. `kubectl` has no cluster access from this machine, so I can't pull them.

One honest caveat on my earlier framing: I said "not the 429" based on `personal-agent` answering in the `buremba` org, and I stand by that — but I haven't proven the Telegram *dispatch* uses that same provider path, so a provider failure that's swallowed rather than surfaced isn't fully excluded. That's also what the logs would settle.

Confidence: **high (90)** that #2257 is deployed and doesn't cover this case — verified by ancestry check and by reading the actual guard. **High (85)** that the drop is post-routing and silent. **Low (20)** on the precise line, unverified without logs.

Next steps you could pick from:
- Get me prod log access (or paste a grep of `85045b7a87884eea` / `"Routing to connection's owning agent"`) — one pass pins it.
- I file an issue capturing this as the sibling of #2230: same silent-drop class, routed path instead of unrouted.
- I add a failing integration test for "connection with `agent_id` + inbound Telegram DM → reply", which would have caught this and gives red→fix→green evidence.
- Separately: the `connect()` vs `create()` silent-dead-connection bug from earlier is still unfixed and is its own PR.

I left three test messages in the Telegram chat and a tab open in your browser — happy to clean up whenever.

---
name: reference_synthetic_events_dont_send_in_react_composers
description: Browser-automation trap — synthetic clicks/Enter silently fail to SEND in React composers (Telegram Web); the text sits as a draft and looks sent.
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Driving a React chat composer (Telegram Web `web.telegram.org/a/`) via the Owletto Chrome
bridge: text can be typed into the composer successfully, but **submitting it silently fails**.

Both of these produced NO sent message on Telegram Web (2026-07-29):
- `click_ref` on the send button from a fresh `get_accessibility_tree` snapshot
- `evaluate` dispatching `new KeyboardEvent('keydown'|'keypress'|'keyup', {key:'Enter',
  keyCode:13, bubbles:true, cancelable:true})` on the contenteditable

React ignores events with `isTrusted: false` for send, so the text just stays in the composer
as a draft. **The failure is invisible** — `document.body.innerText` still shows your text
(because the draft renders inline near the message list), so a naive "did my text appear on
the page?" check reports success and you conclude the remote side dropped the message.

**Verify a send by the message list, never by page text:**
`[...document.querySelectorAll('.message-list-item')].map(m => m.innerText)` — the text must
appear THERE. Also check for a `MessageOutgoingStatus` node. A populated
`#editable-message-text` after a "send" means it never sent.

This cost a wrong conclusion in this session: three "unanswered" Telegram messages had never
actually been sent, which nearly got recorded as a server-side silent-drop bug.
See [[project_slack_telegram_e2e_verify_2026_07_29]].

Workaround: have the human send the message, or use the platform's API directly (for a bot
you own, `sendMessage` only posts AS the bot — it cannot simulate the human side, so an
inbound e2e test genuinely needs a real user action).

Two things were wrong on my side.

First, kubectl worked all along — I used the wrong namespace (`summaries-prod`, and the label is `app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu`, not `lobu-app`). My earlier "no cluster access" was my error.

The draft text still renders near the message list, so my `document.body.innerText` check showed it and I read that as "sent". **My "three messages, no reply" claim was void.** Sorry — that's what drove the confident bug report.

So the answer to "didn't we fix this?" is: **we may well have, and my test never exercised it.** #2257 is real and deployed (prod is `049ee2ab`; `git merge-base --is-ancestor` confirms). If Telegram dispatch routes through that proxy path, the quota is a live suspect for the `/start` silence.

The honest status: Telegram is connected and wired correctly (webhook registered, secret enforced, agent bound), and it's **unverified**, not proven broken.

Confidence: **high (90)** that my three follow-ups never sent — verified against the message list. **High (85)** that #2257 is deployed and doesn't apply here. **Low (15)** on any claim that Telegram inbound is broken; I'm retracting that.

**You're right that Chat SDK provides everything — and it does. There is no Chat SDK gap.** The adapter (`@chat-adapter/telegram@4.26.0`) verifies the secret, parses the update, and calls `chat.processMessage()`. All correct.

**The `/start` message did arrive and was handled.** I found the real delivery in the logs: `POST /lobu/api/v1/webhooks/85045b7a87884eea` from `91.108.5.129` (Telegram's IP), valid secret header, 288-byte body, **HTTP 200**. Not dropped at the edge.

But here's the thing that changes the diagnosis: **`/start` is the wrong test.** Telegram sends it as a bot command; there's no agent turn to run and no reply expected. Nothing in the logs after that delivery shows *any* Telegram processing — no `unified-thread-consumer` for `platform=telegram`. Every entry in that window is `platform=api` / `watcher_5`.

And the `watcher_5` runs in that same window are the real story:

```

[api-response-renderer] Broadcast error to session personal-agent_watcher_5_run_784313:
         z.ai returned an error: 429 Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted
```

The one genuine code smell I did find: `postToPayloadTarget` (`chat-response-bridge.ts:851`) does `if (target) await target.post(content)` — **if target resolution returns null, it silently does nothing**, no log, no throw. x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token: b2576236…   (valid)

And then **nothing**. No `"Processing inbound message"`, no `platform=telegram`, anywhere in the following 90 seconds. Only unrelated `watcher_5` work.

So this kills my previous `/start` theory. A plain text message is dropped too. The adapter accepts it, ACKs 200, and it never reaches `MessageHandlerBridge.handleMessage`. The drop is inside Chat SDK's `handleIncomingMessage` → `dispatchToHandlers`, whose early returns — `isMe`, dedupe, and the `handleDrop` lock-conflict path — **all log at `debug`, while prod runs at `info`**. That's why it's invisible.

The strongest clue is `responseTime: 1079ms` for parsing a 279-byte JSON body. That's far too slow for parse-and-dispatch, and it matches an `acquireLock` / state-adapter round-trip. My prime suspect is the `handleDrop` lock conflict or the `dedupe:` key in the Postgres state adapter — plausibly a stale lock from the connection's creation that never cleared.

I'm stopping before the fix, deliberately. I have the failure reproduced but not the *line*, and the three candidate causes need different fixes. That settles it. Direct answer: **no, we shouldn't add it everywhere — the flag is correct as-is.**

The SDK's own contract says why:

> "When true, the SDK persists message history in the state adapter for this platform. Use this for platforms that lack server-side message history APIs (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram)."

It's a **capability compensation flag**, not a feature toggle. Telegram and WhatsApp have no server-side history API — a bot can't ask Telegram "what was said in this chat before?", so the SDK caches it locally. Slack, Discord, Teams, and GChat all have `conversations.history`-style APIs, so caching there would be duplicated state that can go stale. The flag being set on exactly Telegram + WhatsApp and absent on the other four is the SDK doing the right thing. Adding it everywhere would *create* tech debt, not remove it.

So the flag isn't the bug. **The bug is that a best-effort cache write can kill message delivery.** Here's the actual defect, in `chat/dist/index.js:2966`:

```js
if (adapter.persistMessageHistory) {
  await this._messageHistory.append(threadId, message);  // throws → whole turn dies
}
...
await this.handleDrop(...)   // never reached
```

A history-cache write is a nice-to-have. It sits *upstream* of dispatch with no try/catch, so when it throws, the user's message is silently discarded. That's the design flaw — and it's in the SDK, not our code. It only bites Telegram/WhatsApp because they're the only platforms that execute that line, which is exactly why Slack has been fine this whole time.

On your tech-debt framing, the thing worth consolidating is the **three-layer swallow** that made this take all night to find:

1. Chat SDK runs a best-effort side-effect before dispatch, unguarded.
2. `processMessage` catches everything and logs at `debug`.
3. `chat-instance-manager.ts:1553` hardcodes `logger: "warn"`, so debug is unreachable in prod — no env var can turn it on.

Net effect: a swallowed exception, an invisible log, and a 200 back to Telegram. The message is gone with zero trace. Add `postToPayloadTarget`'s silent no-op on a null target and that's four places where a failure produces nothing.

What I'd fix, smallest to most valuable:

- **Unpin the logger** (`logger: "warn"` → driven by `LOG_LEVEL`). One line. Makes this whole class visible instead of requiring a night of black-box probing.
- **Make the history write non-fatal.** It's a cache; a failure must not drop the message. Cleanest is upstream in the SDK, but we can guard at our boundary until then.
- **Stop `postToPayloadTarget` silently no-op'ing** — log when target resolution returns null.

I still owe you *why* the append throws for this specific chat. With the logger unpinned, one message answers it — versus me continuing to guess between a `chat_state_lists` seq/trim failure and a serialization issue.

Want me to open that PR? Scope: unpin the logger, guard the history write, fix the null-target swallow, plus the reproducer harness I already have working. That kills the class rather than patching a symptom — which is the consolidation you're asking for.

content.text:
Your instinct was right, and it points at a cleaner long-term fix than what I proposed earlier.

**We do have message history in the DB, and it's the better store.** `captureChannelMessage` → `channel_messages` (`channel-transcript.ts`) is platform-agnostic, idempotent, org-scoped, and — critically — **fire-and-forget with a `.catch()` that logs a warning and moves on**. It exists precisely so `read_conversation` serves from Postgres instead of the throttled platform APIs. That's the right design, and it's already shipped.

**The SDK cache is dead code that can kill delivery.** I grepped for consumers of the SDK's `messageHistory` cache across the whole server: **zero**. Nothing reads it. Meanwhile `readChannelTranscript` has three real consumers (`manage_feeds`, the internal conversations route, `read_conversation`).

So we're maintaining two history stores. One is ours, durable, queryable cross-platform, and safe to fail. The other is the SDK's per-thread cache in `chat_state_lists`, read by nobody, written **before** dispatch with no try/catch — so when it throws, your message is silently discarded. That's how one redundant write took down Telegram while Slack was unaffected (Slack never executes that line).

**Best long-term fix: delete the redundant store, don't guard it.** Concretely:

1. **Stop the SDK from persisting history.** Nothing reads it, so this is a pure deletion — not a shim, not a fallback. It removes the failure mode at the source rather than wrapping it in try/catch. `Chat` takes a `messageHistory` config option, so there's a supported lever; if it can't be fully disabled from config, that's a one-line upstream change to make the append non-fatal, and we pin until it lands.
2. **`channel_messages` becomes the single source of truth** for "pull all conversations across everywhere" — which is what you already built it for, and it already works on every platform.
3. **Unpin `logger: "warn"`** at `chat-instance-manager.ts:1553` so SDK-internal drops are visible via `LOG_LEVEL`. This is what cost us the whole night: the exception was caught and logged at `debug`, which no env var could reach.

That's genuine consolidation — two stores become one, and the deletion removes the bug class instead of papering over it. It also satisfies the deletion-evidence bar in AGENTS.md: zero consumers is structural evidence, not a usage guess.

One caveat I won't paper over: I've confirmed the *mechanism* (pre-dispatch append throws → swallowed → 200 → silence, reproduced locally with identical symptoms, and prod is missing the `msg-history:telegram:8450689116` row). I have **not** confirmed *why* it throws for this chat. Deleting the write makes that moot — but if it's something like a DB-level failure on `chat_state_lists`, the same root cause could surface elsewhere. Unpinning the logger first tells us in one message, and it's worth knowing before we delete.

Suggested PR order: unpin the logger → send one Telegram message → capture the real exception → then delete the redundant history write with the reproducer as the red test. That's one worktree and a small diff, with red→fix→green evidence rather than a speculative fix.

/**
 * Force every adapter onto one inbound path by turning off the Chat SDK's
 * own message-history cache.
 *
 * The SDK writes that cache inside `handleIncomingMessage` BEFORE it
 * dispatches to handlers, gated only on the adapter's `persistMessageHistory`
 * flag, and with no try/catch. `processMessage` swallows whatever it throws
 * and still answers the platform 200, so a failing *cache* write silently
 * discards the user's message. Telegram and WhatsApp set the flag; Slack,
 * Discord, Teams and GChat do not — so the same build dropped Telegram DMs
 * while Slack was unaffected, which is exactly the kind of per-platform
 * divergence this seam exists to prevent.
 *
 * Turning it off costs nothing: Lobu persists its own transcripts via
 * `captureChannelMessage` → `channel_messages` (platform-agnostic, idempotent,
 * fire-and-forget), which is what `read_conversation` and the conversations
 * route actually read. The SDK cache has no readers in this repo, so it was
 * pure risk. Disabling it here — at the one chokepoint every platform's
 * adapter passes through — keeps inbound dispatch identical everywhere.
 */
export function disableSdkMessageHistory<T>(adapter: T): T {
  // `persistMessageHistory` is declared readonly on the SDK interface, so
  // redefine rather than assign; some adapters expose it on the prototype.
  Object.defineProperty(adapter as object, "persistMessageHistory", {
    value: false,
    configurable: true,
    enumerable: true,
    writable: true,
  });
  return adapter;
}

content.text:
You're right and I corrected the design mid-flight. Here's the honest accounting.

**Where I landed: 56 insertions / 4 deletions — still net-positive, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.** But the structural direction is what you asked for: it removes a write path and eliminates a per-platform divergence.

**Why I can't just delete the flag.** `@chat-adapter/*` and `chat` are Vercel's upstream SDK (`github.com/vercel/chat`), pinned at `^4.26.0`. `persistMessageHistory` is declared on their `ChatAdapter` interface and the cache is constructed unconditionally inside `Chat` — there's no config switch to disable it. So the knob isn't ours to remove; the only lever on our side is to neutralize it at the one chokepoint every adapter passes through (`createAdapter`). The alternative is an upstream PR, which I'd support but can't gate this fix on.

**What it actually consolidates**, which is the part that matters more than line count:

- Every adapter now takes an **identical** inbound path. Today Telegram/WhatsApp run a pre-dispatch write that Slack/Discord/Teams/GChat don't — that divergence is exactly why Telegram broke while Slack was fine on the same build.
- It **deletes a write**, it doesn't add one. Nothing reads `msg-history:*` — I grepped for `getMessages`/`msg-history` across the server: zero consumers. Our real transcripts go to `channel_messages` via `captureChannelMessage`.
- It removes a whole failure mode: a *cache* write can no longer drop a user's message.

**One thing I found while checking your point, and it changed my plan:** I was about to make `appendToList` non-fatal in `LobuStateAdapter` — fewer lines, no new function. That would have been wrong. `conversation-state-store.ts` also writes through `appendToList`, and that store **is** read back (`getEntries`, `listHistoryChannels`). Blanket-swallowing there would hide real failures. So the narrow seam is correct, not just convenient.

I also trimmed my own over-explaining — the helper's comment went from 20 lines to 11, and I dropped a redundant `enumerable`.

Evidence so far, per AGENTS.md:
- **Red:** 2 pass / 2 fail — both failures at `chat/dist/index.js:2966` in `handleIncomingMessage`, pre-dispatch.
- **Green:** 5 pass / 0 fail.
- **Mutation-tested:** flipping `value: false` → `true` re-breaks the drop test, so the test genuinely bites.

Two things I'd like your call on, since they're scope decisions:

1. **Deleting the ~48 orphaned `msg-history:*` rows in prod.** They become permanently dead after this. That's real net-negative cleanup, but it's a prod data deletion so I won't do it unattended.
2. **`ConversationStateStore` vs `channel_messages`** — these are two overlapping history stores, and *that's* the big consolidation worth a net-negative diff. It has ~12 call sites across the manager and bridge, so it's its own branch (one branch = one concern), not this one.

cd /Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/.claude/worktrees/chat-history-consolidation; cat > /tmp/pr-body.md <<'EOF'
## What

The Chat SDK writes its message-history cache inside `handleIncomingMessage`
**before** dispatching to handlers, gated only on the adapter's
`persistMessageHistory` flag and with no `try/catch`. `processMessage` swallows
whatever it throws and the webhook still answers `200`, so a failing *cache*
write silently discards the user's message.

Only Telegram and WhatsApp set that flag; Slack, Discord, Teams and GChat do
not — so the same build dropped Telegram DMs while Slack was fine. That is a
per-platform divergence in the one path that must be identical everywhere.

Nothing reads that cache. Lobu's durable transcripts go to `channel_messages`
via `captureChannelMessage` (platform-agnostic, idempotent, fire-and-forget),
which is what `read_conversation` and the conversations route actually query.
`grep` for `getMessages`/`msg-history` across `packages/server/src` returns zero
consumers.

Fix: normalize the flag off in `createAdapter` — the single chokepoint every
platform's adapter passes through — so inbound dispatch is identical for all six
adapters. This removes a write path; it does not add one.

Also stops hardcoding the SDK logger to `"warn"`. Every SDK-internal inbound
drop (duplicate, lock conflict, and the `processMessage` catch-all) logs at
`debug`, so the pin made these failures invisible at any `LOG_LEVEL` — which is
why this took a production investigation to find.

## Production evidence

A real Telegram DM to `@burembalobubot` (connection 459):

```
POST /lobu/api/v1/webhooks/85045b7a87884eea
cf-connecting-ip: 91.108.5.129        (Telegram)
x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token: ...  (valid)
content-length: 279  ->  res.status: 200, responseTime: 1079ms
```

`200` returned, no `"Processing inbound message"`, no `platform=telegram`
anywhere after it — the bridge was never reached. `getWebhookInfo` reported no
delivery error, so Telegram considered it delivered. Slack on the same build
was unaffected.

## Red -> green

Red (before the fix), both failures at `chat/dist/index.js:2966` inside
`handleIncomingMessage`, before dispatch:

```
(fail) inbound dispatch parity across chat adapters > a failing history store must NOT drop the message
(fail) inbound dispatch parity across chat adapters > delivery is identical whether or not the adapter persists history
 2 pass
 2 fail
```

Green (after):

```
 3 pass
 0 fail
Ran 3 tests across 1 file.
```

Mutation-tested: flipping `value: false` -> `true` in `disableSdkMessageHistory`
re-breaks the drop test, so the test bites.

`raw SDK drops the message when history persistence fails` pins *why* the seam
exists — if it ever starts delivering, the SDK fixed it upstream and the seam
can go.

## Test plan

- [x] `make pre-pr` clean
- [x] `make test-unit` — 156 + 163 + 4 pass, 0 fail
- [x] `make review-fix` applied and diff verified
- [ ] Prod: Telegram DM gets a reply; Slack still replies; pages render
EOF

## RESOLVED — PR #2305 (squash `63c7dd519`), merged 2026-07-29

**Root cause.** Chat SDK writes its message-history cache inside
`handleIncomingMessage` **before** `dispatchToHandlers`, gated only on the adapter's
`persistMessageHistory` flag and with **no try/catch** (`chat/dist/index.js:2966`).
`processMessage` catches the throw and the webhook still answers **200**, so a failing
*cache* write silently discards the user's message. Only **telegram + whatsapp** set that
flag (`slack/discord/teams/gchat` do not) — which is exactly why Telegram DMs vanished
while Slack worked on the same build.

**Fix.** Normalize the flag off in `ChatInstanceManager.createAdapter()` — the single
chokepoint every platform's adapter passes through — via `disableSdkMessageHistory()` in
`gateway/connections/platforms/shared.ts`. Removes a write path, does not add one:
nothing reads that cache (grep `getMessages`/`msg-history` in packages/server/src → zero
consumers). Lobu's durable transcripts are `channel_messages` via `captureChannelMessage`
(3 real consumers). Also unpinned the hardcoded `logger: "warn"` → honours `LOG_LEVEL`.
Review: bug_free 96, simplicity 95, slop 0, 0 blockers.

**Do NOT "add persistMessageHistory everywhere".** It is a capability-compensation flag,
not a feature toggle — the SDK sets it only for platforms with no server-side history API
(its own docstring says so). Adding it broadly would create duplicated stale state.

content.text:
Monitor armed for the rollout. Here's where things stand.

## Shipped: PR #2305 merged (`63c7dd519`)

**Root cause found and fixed.** Chat SDK writes its message-history cache inside `handleIncomingMessage` **before** dispatching to handlers, gated on the adapter's `persistMessageHistory` flag, with **no try/catch** (`chat/dist/index.js:2966`). `processMessage` swallows the throw and the webhook still answers 200 — so a failing *cache* write silently discards the user's message.

Only **telegram and whatsapp** set that flag. That's the whole asymmetry: same build, Telegram DMs vanished, Slack was fine.

**The consolidation you asked for.** I normalize the flag off in `createAdapter()` — the single chokepoint every platform's adapter passes through. Verified on real constructed instances:

```
telegram  before=true   after=false
whatsapp  before=true   after=false
slack / discord / teams / gchat — never set it
```

All six adapters now take an identical inbound path. This **removes a write path rather than adding one**: nothing reads that cache (grep for `getMessages`/`msg-history` across `packages/server/src` → zero consumers), while our real transcripts go to `channel_messages` via `captureChannelMessage`, which has three consumers.

You were right to push back on the knob, and it changed the work: I'd been about to make `appendToList` non-fatal in `LobuStateAdapter` — fewer lines, but **wrong**, because `conversation-state-store.ts` also writes through it and *is* read back. Blanket-swallowing would have hidden real failures. Your question is what surfaced that.

On net-negative: the diff is +205/−3, and I won't dress that up. The upstream flag belongs to Vercel's `chat` package, so I can't delete it — only neutralize it at our seam. The genuinely net-negative consolidation is `ConversationStateStore` vs `channel_messages` (two overlapping stores, ~12 call sites), which is its own branch per one-branch-one-concern.

**Evidence:** red 2 pass/2 fail (both dying at `chat/dist/index.js:2966`) → green 3/3, mutation-tested. `make pre-pr` clean, all 8 required checks pass, review **bug_free 96 / simplicity 95 / slop 0 / 0 blockers**.

**Prod verified so far:**
- All four pages render in a real browser with no error boundary — connectors/telegram shows the live connection, memory shows real counts (Person 4358, Company 2035).
- Slack unaffected: post-merge DM produced `Processing inbound message` in 2s — exactly the line that never appeared for Telegram.

**Not yet done:** Telegram inbound e2e. Prod is on `2df9eb5f`; my build was superseded by `cc269333e` (which contains my fix) and that image is still building. Monitor is armed — when it lands I'll send a Telegram DM and confirm `Processing inbound message` + `platform=telegram`.

One thing you'll want to know regardless: **the Z_AI quota is exhausted until 2026-07-31**, hitting both orgs. Dispatch will be provable via logs, but a visible reply needs a fallback provider — you have `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` set. I didn't add it since that's a prod config change.

input.new_string:
**IT DOES WORK — the real trap is `filter: "interactive"` on the a11y tree.**
Later in the same session I sent Telegram messages successfully via the Owletto bridge. The
send button is **absent from `get_accessibility_tree` with `filter: "interactive"`**, while a
*different* button ("Go to bottom") sits at almost the same coordinates — so geometry-based or
fuzzy-name matching clicks the wrong element and silently does nothing.

Recipe that works:
1. `get_accessibility_tree` with **`filter: "all"`** (not "interactive").
2. Find the composer by exact name match: `(n.name||'').trim().toLowerCase() === 'message'`.
3. `click_ref` it, then `type_ref` the text.
4. Re-snapshot with `filter: "all"` (the send button only appears once there is text).
5. Find send by **exact** name: `=== 'send message'`. Never fuzzy-match `/send/i` and never
   fall back to bounding-box proximity — both hit "Go to bottom".
6. `click_ref` it, then confirm via `.message-list-item` + an emptied composer.

Note `Object.defineProperty`-style state: after each send the epoch changes, so always
re-snapshot before the next interaction rather than reusing a stale `document_epoch`.

Direct API is still no substitute for an inbound test: for a bot you own, `sendMessage` posts
AS the bot, so it cannot simulate the human side.

content.text:
Done. Telegram works end to end in production, and all six chat adapters now share one inbound path.

## The bug

Chat SDK writes its message-history cache inside `handleIncomingMessage` **before** dispatching to handlers, gated on the adapter's `persistMessageHistory` flag, with **no try/catch** (`chat/dist/index.js:2966`). `processMessage` swallows the throw and the webhook still answers 200 — so a failing *cache* write silently discarded the user's message.

Only **telegram and whatsapp** set that flag. That's the entire asymmetry: same build, Telegram DMs vanished, Slack was fine.

## The fix — one path, not a new knob

Normalized the flag off at `createAdapter()`, the single chokepoint every platform's adapter passes through. Verified on real constructed instances:

```
telegram  before=true   after=false
whatsapp  before=true   after=false
slack / discord / teams / gchat — never set it
```

This **removes a write path rather than adding one**: nothing read that cache (zero consumers for `getMessages`/`msg-history`), while our durable transcripts go to `channel_messages`, which has three real consumers. Also unpinned the hardcoded `logger: "warn"` — every SDK silent-drop path logs at `debug`, so that pin is what made this undiagnosable.

Your pushback changed the design twice. The "why a new knob" question stopped me shipping a neutralizer where a deletion belonged, and it also caught me about to make `appendToList` non-fatal in `LobuStateAdapter` — fewer lines, but **wrong**, because `conversation-state-store.ts` writes through it and *is* read back.

## Proof in prod

```
[chat-message-bridge] Processing inbound message          ← never appeared pre-fix
[platform-helpers]    Routing to connection's owning agent
[queue-producer]      Enqueued message job 786981, conversation telegram:8450689116
[worker] User prompt: POSTFIX9 verify dispatch...
```

And `channel_messages` has its **first-ever** `platform='telegram'` rows, both directions — inbound id 69, **agent reply id 70** (`is_bot=true`) seven seconds later. The identical webhook shape previously returned 200 and produced nothing.

Slack re-verified unaffected. All four pages render with live data (Person 4358, Company 2035).

Gates: `make pre-pr` clean, 8/8 required checks, review **96/95/slop 0/0 blockers**, red 2-fail → green 3-pass, mutation-tested. Merged as `63c7dd519`, rolled out in `cc269333e`.

**One thing needs your decision:** the Z_AI quota is exhausted until **2026-07-31** and intermittently fails turns in both orgs.
